html:
The Berlin Conference was a meeting of fourteen countries in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885 that set rules for European claims to Africa. Otto von Bismarck, chancellor of Germany, hosted it at the request of Leopold II of Belgium. No Africans took part.

It ended with the General Act of Berlin:

  • free trade in the Congo basin and free navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers;
  • a rule that a power claiming a stretch of African coast must tell the others and hold it by "effective occupation";
  • promises to end the slave trade and protect Africans, which were mostly ignored.

Around the conference the powers recognised Leopold's claim to the Congo basin, which became his private Congo Free State. His rule there became notorious for forced rubber collection, mutilation and mass death.

A common story says the conference drew Africa's borders. It did not; most borders were fixed later in treaties between pairs of powers. But it set the terms for the Scramble for Africa. By 1914 almost the whole continent was under European rule. Only Liberia and the Ethiopian Empire, which beat Italy at Adwa, stayed independent.
